notes: FALSIFIED FIRST, against the shipped code, before writing a line of the fix: a 6-boundary pair cut from the REAL scripts/verification-boundaries.v1.json (both sides well-formed, 2800 and 2743 bytes) through the current tool gave 'ours=101 theirs=100 theirs_only=2 result=62 sorted_by_ts=False' and EXIT 0, and the output does not parse (json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Expecting ',' delimiter). Same mechanism as the 182 KB -> 96 KB incident, same class of error, and the sizes are in the same ratio. The mechanism is exact and not a guess: the dedup collapses the repeated structural lines ('{', '},', '],'), so 201 physical lines become 62 and every comma/brace position moves.

THE FIX IS A REFUSAL, NOT A SMARTER MERGE, and that is a design-gate decision rather than a shortcut: a second JSON merge implementation would be a parallel fork of boundary-union logic the manager plane already owns in TWO places with CONFLICTING rules (union-registry-sides.py: ours wins, differences reported, exit 3; union-verification-registry.py: refuse if any shared entry differs, textual insertion, validate-before-write). Choosing between them is a product decision this tool must not make by accident. So --structured was NOT built; the refusal message names the right tool per class instead. That is the thin delegation - a pointer, not an implementation.

The refusal is decided from TWO independent signals, because the measured incident arrived with the sides named ours.txt / theirs.txt (resolve-append-only.ps1:38-39 renames both sides before calling) while --out kept the real name. A suffix rule alone misses a registry merged to a .txt; a content probe alone misses a mislabelled file. Both refuse, and either one alone is enough.

The content probe runs on the MARKER-STRIPPED text, not the raw file, so a conflicted working file full of <<<<<<< markers cannot hide a document's shape from it. This closes the hole union-verification-registry.py's own docstring describes (it parses an invalid document and refuses - correct behaviour, unhelpful timing).

STATED TRADE-OFF, chosen deliberately: a one-line-per-side file whose content parses as a single JSON document is refused when its name carries no .jsonl suffix. That is a minified structured file more often than a degenerate ledger, and a one-line append-only ledger cannot conflict in the first place (there is nothing to append). The refusal message names the reason so an operator sees it immediately.

NO OVERRIDE FLAG, on purpose. An --allow-structured escape hatch is exactly how the destructive path gets reopened by the next agent who is in a hurry; a named refusal with a named remedy is the cheaper answer.

ROUND TRIP IS A WRITE-PATH PROPERTY, not a promise: the union is written to a sibling staged file, re-read and re-validated there, and only then os.replace'd onto the destination. A refusal therefore leaves the destination byte-identical to what it was - which is the difference between the incident (a 96 KB corrupt registry sitting in the tree, reported as success) and a refusal. Verified: the structured-input refusal leaves the --out path absent.

HONEST LIMIT OF THE ROUND-TRIP EVIDENCE: by construction the two round-trip predicates (re-read lines equal the built lines; a jsonl output re-parses row by row) cannot fail from the CLI once the pre-write checks pass, so they are NOT end-to-end tested - they are unit-tested as predicates with crafted corrupt input, and the temp-write helper is unit-tested with an injected failing validator (which also proves the destination is untouched and no staged file is left). Saying so beats claiming a CLI green that is unreachable.

APPEND-ONLY PARITY is measured, not asserted: the current tool's output on a real tasks/ ledger and a real tasks/*-todo.md pair is saved as the before-image, and the fixed tool's output is diffed against it. Both are byte-identical; the only difference is the human summary line, which gained the shape and round-trip fields the brief asked for, and --json now exists.
